# The Machine Anatomy {.unnumbered}

\lettrine{E}{very} physical AI system is defined by the physical apparatus through which it acts. An advisory computation can end at a display or a human decision, although an erroneous output may still cause harm when acted upon. Physical AI operates across a causal threshold where permitted commands drive current, force, and motion. Matter will not pause while an operating system schedules a thread, and a later software rollback cannot undo work already delivered into the plant or environment.

::: {#pri-vol4-irreversibility .callout-principle title="The irreversibility invariant"}

**Invariant**: A proposal can be rejected before actuation, but software rollback cannot reverse motion or dissipated heat after a command has delivered physical work. Idempotency describes the effect of repeating a command; it does not imply that its physical effects are reversible. If the plant continues at constant speed $v_0$ without braking during a sense-to-brake delay $\Delta t_{\text{delay}}$, the reaction displacement is
$$ d_{\text{react}} = v_0 \cdot \Delta t_{\text{delay}} $$
With an additional constant braking deceleration $a_{\text{max}}>0$, stationary obstacle, and no unmodeled brake-onset delay, the model gives $d_{\text{stop}} = v_0 \cdot \Delta t_{\text{delay}} + \frac{v_0^2}{2 a_{\text{max}}}$. A stop before the obstacle requires $d_{\text{stop}} \le d_{\text{clear}}$ under those assumptions.

**Implication**: A software exception handler cannot stop moving mass. The permission path must have an independently enforced response budget, a veto, and a physical fallback. A measured $p99.9$ latency can inform that budget but is not a worst-case bound; the chosen deadline must also account for sensing error, brake onset, and actuator limits.

:::

To engineer systems that survive in the physical world, Part I establishes the **Constraint-Driven Architecture** of physical AI. Rather than treating an autonomous machine as an abstract software pipeline, we ground the entire discipline in the structural triad (Body, Brain, Nervous System) and its operational counterpart, the **S·P·A (Sense, Plan, Act)** framework (@sec-boundary-spa-triad, @sec-appendix-spa):

* **The Body (@sec-body):** The physical, mechanical, and thermal plant. Its motion and energy flows obey mechanics and electromagnetism rather than software instructions. Stopping clearance, reflected rotor inertia ($N^2 J$), winding heat ($I^2 R$), and voltage droop constrain what it can execute; sensor freshness constrains how accurately the other tiers know its state.
* **The Brain (@sec-brain):** The learned cognitive deliberative engine. We define what the brain is *for*—high-capacity open-world semantic generalization, spatial affordance extraction, and continuous trajectory synthesis that classical hand-crafted state machines cannot achieve. Crucially, we also define what *bounds* the brain: the memory wall, Roofline arithmetic intensity limits, stochastic fat-tailed latency, and uncalibrated confidence. Because of these constraints, the brain must operate as an **unprivileged proposal engine**, emitting advisory action chunks rather than direct actuator commands.
* **The Nervous System (@sec-nervous):** The real-time architectural bridge. Between a slower brain (for example, $1\text{--}10\text{ Hz}$) and faster local control (for example, $1000\text{ Hz}$), it arbitrates time and authority. It checks proposals against state-dependent limits and executes a defined fallback when high-level software stalls. A Control Barrier Function can support such a check when its plant model, state estimate, and feasible control authority satisfy the conditions of its guarantee.

::: {#pri-vol4-proposal-boundary .callout-principle title="The proposal boundary"}

**Invariant**: A learned cognitive model proposes candidate action trajectories; it does not hold direct write access to actuator power stages. An independent permission mechanism accepts, modifies, or vetoes each proposal before actuation and retains authority to execute a fallback if the proposer fails. The cited $1\text{--}10\text{ Hz}$ deliberation and $1000\text{ Hz}$ reflex rates are implementation examples, not universal requirements.

**Implication**: The proposal and permission paths need fault containment, a bounded communication delay, and a fallback that does not wait on the failed proposer. Asynchronous buffers and a separate controller are one implementation. If a proposal is stale or unsafe, the permission path rejects it and executes a validated braking or risk-reducing maneuver within the available physical margin; stopping is possible only while sufficient clearance and control authority remain.

:::

::: {#pri-vol4-physical-budgets .callout-principle title="The plant budget contract"}

**Invariant**: Five coupled engineering constraints bound a specified operating state; they are not five conservation laws. Measurement age must remain within a validated state-estimation horizon ($\Delta t_{\text{age}} \le \tau_{\text{valid}}$), and stopping distance must fit measured clearance ($d_{\text{stop}} \le d_{\text{clear}}$) under stated sensing and braking assumptions. For ideal rigid gearing, reflected rotor inertia is $J_{\text{ref}} = N^2 J_m$. For a lumped winding with no credited cooling, resistive heating must fit its thermal margin ($\int I_{\text{phase}}^2 R_{\text{phase}} \, dt \le C_{\text{th}} \Delta T_{\text{max}}$). For a simplified unbuffered bus during rising current, estimated voltage must stay above the operating minimum ($V_{\text{bus}} - L_{\text{bus}} \frac{dI_{\text{bus}}}{dt} - I_{\text{bus}} R_{\text{bus}} \ge V_{\text{min}}$). Model error, saturation, cooling, and protection behavior determine whether these approximations are conservative enough for a given machine.

**Implication**: An optimization that consumes any one margin can increase contact force, winding temperature, voltage sag, or stopping distance. The design must identify which budget binds first, measure its uncertainty, and allocate sensing, derating, buffering, or fallback capacity before permitting a proposal.

:::

Part I provides the mental models, systems napkin math, and architectural foundations required to understand this Triad. Before we collect demonstrations, train neural policies, or build runtime perception stacks, we must first master the physical constraints that dictate how a machine survives in the material world.
